title: Third-he roots and shortened forms

objectives.can: Recognise forms of roots ending in ה, including the shortened forms of the jussive and wayyiqtol.

explanation.summary: Many of the commonest Hebrew verbs, among them הָיָה, עָשָׂה and רָאָה, end in ה in their dictionary form. That ה is not a real consonant. It is a vowel letter, and the root's true last consonant shows only before some endings. In the wayyiqtol and the jussive the ending is cut off altogether, which is why וַיַּרְא and וַיְהִי look so short.

sections.heading: A final ה that is not a consonant
body: Take the verb עָשָׂה, 'do, make'. Its last letter ה is not pronounced as a consonant: it only marks the vowel ָ before it. Grammarians call roots of this kind third-he roots, or lamed-he roots, because the third root letter is written ה. In most of them the last root consonant was originally י (a few had ו), and that older consonant comes back in some forms.

You can see it when the ending begins with a consonant. In Genesis 3:14 God says to the serpent כִּי עָשִׂיתָ זֹּאת, 'because you have done this'. The ending -תָּ is the 2nd masculine singular of the qatal, and the י of the root appears between the stem and the ending: עָשִׂיתָ. In the verse before, the woman is asked מַה זֹּאת עָשִׂית, with the 2nd feminine singular עָשִׂית. The same י stands in עָשִׂיתִי, 'I did', and עָשִׂינוּ, 'we did'.

sections.heading: Before vowel endings the ה is dropped
body: When an ending begins with a vowel, the ה is simply lost. The 3rd plural qatal is עָשׂוּ, 'they made', not a form with ה in it, and the 3rd plural yiqtol is יַעֲשׂוּ. The same happens with the feminine ending, where the vowel of the stem also shortens: עָשְׂתָה, 'she made'.

This is the first thing to look for when the ending of a form does not match the dictionary headword. If a form has no ה at its end, and the root seems to have only two letters, test whether the headword might be a third-he verb. A form such as רָאוּ, 'they saw', has the root letters ר א (and a missing third); the headword רָאָה supplies it.

sections.heading: Shortened forms: the wayyiqtol and the jussive
body: The yiqtol of a third-he verb ends in -ֶה: יַעֲשֶׂה, יִבְנֶה, יִרְאֶה, יִהְיֶה. When the same prefix form is used in the wayyiqtol or the jussive, the ending is cut off. Grammarians call this apocope (cutting off). The result is a short form with no ה.

Because the ending has gone, the form often ends in two consonants, or a helping vowel appears to break up the cluster. That is why וַיִּבֶן 'and he built' ends in a segol before the נ, and why וַיַּרְא 'and he saw' ends in the cluster רְא.

sections.heading: Where the shortening shows and where it does not
body: The shortening is regular in the 3rd person singular, and the feminine 3rd person shows it too: וַתֵּרֶא, 'and she saw', וַתַּעַשׂ, 'and she made'. It also appears in the 1st person singular wayyiqtol, as in וָאֵרֶא, 'and I saw'. In the plural the ה has already gone before the ending -וּ, so the wayyiqtol plural looks like the yiqtol plural with וַ in front: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ, 'and they made', וַיִּבְנוּ, 'and they built'. There is nothing shortened to notice.

To find the root of a short form, remove the prefix (וַיִּ-, וַיַּ-, וַתֵּ-) and see what is left. For וַיִּפֶן what is left is פ נ, only two root consonants. A lexicon will show which verbs have פ נ and a ה: פָּנָה. Two consonants after the prefix is the signal to test the third-he roots.

sections.heading: Stems other than the Qal
body: The same changes happen in the other stems. In Genesis 8:20 the verb וַיַּעַל is a Hiphil of the same root עָלָה (the offering is made to go up), and it is shortened in just the same way as the Qal. Several third-he verbs are much commoner in a derived stem than in the Qal: צָוָה, 'command', occurs mostly in the Piel. Whatever the stem, look for the same signs: a missing final ה in the wayyiqtol and jussive, a returning י before consonant endings.

misunderstandings: The final ה of עָשָׂה is not a feminine ending and not the third root consonant in the sound of the word. The 3rd masculine singular qatal ends in -ָה just as the 3rd feminine singular of an ordinary verb does, and only the context and the stem tell them apart.

A short wayyiqtol such as וַיַּרְא is not a different verb or a different tense from the long yiqtol יִרְאֶה. It is the same prefix form with its ending cut off, the shape the wayyiqtol regularly takes in this class of root.

A shortened form does not by itself prove a jussive. The wayyiqtol takes the same short shape. What decides is the וַ in front, and the context: the wayyiqtol tells what happened, and the jussive expresses a wish or command.
The root does not always have a ה. In forms like עָשִׂיתָ or בָּנוּי the last root consonant is י. Do not look for ה in the middle of the form.

deeper.heading: Why the ending is cut off
body: Grammarians generally explain the short forms as the survival of an older, shorter shape of the prefix form, which is still found in the jussive and in the wayyiqtol. This is one standard description of a very old pattern, and the grammars listed among the course sources set it out in detail. For reading, what matters is the practical rule: where the yiqtol has -ֶה, the wayyiqtol and the shortened jussive have none.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament; and it was so.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two wayyiqtols of third-he roots in one verse. וַיַּעַשׂ is the Qal wayyiqtol 3rd masculine singular of עָשָׂה: 'and he made'. The long yiqtol would be יַעֲשֶׂה; here the ending is gone. וַיְהִי is the same kind of form from הָיָה: 'and it was'. Only י and ה of the prefix and the first root letter remain, with a shewa where the stem has no full vowel.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he smote the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two shortened wayyiqtols that show the cluster at the end of the word. וַיִּפֶן, 'and he turned', is from פָּנָה: after the prefix only פ נ is left, with a helping segol between them. וַיַּרְא, 'and he saw', is from רָאָה: it ends in the cluster רְא, with no ה.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the LORD God said unto the serpent: 'Because thou hast done this, cursed art thou from among all cattle, and from among all beasts of the field; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: עָשִׂיתָ is the Qal qatal 2nd masculine singular of עָשָׂה. The ה of the headword has gone, and the older י of the root stands between the stem and the ending -תָּ. This returning י is the sign of a third-he verb before an ending that begins with a consonant.

quoted.title: 2 Samuel
quoted.english: And the king said unto Araunah: 'Nay; but I will verily buy it of thee at a price; neither will I offer burnt-offerings unto the LORD my God which cost me nothing.' So David bought the threshing-floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two forms of the root קָנָה, 'buy', in one verse. אֶקְנֶה is a Qal yiqtol, 1st singular: the ending -ֶה is still there, and the speaker says what he will do. וַיִּקֶן is the Qal wayyiqtol 3rd masculine singular: the ending is gone, and it tells what David did. Same root, same prefix conjugation, and the ending shows which one is which.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Noah builded an altar unto the LORD; and took of every clean beast, and of every clean fowl, and offered burnt-offerings on the altar.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וַיִּבֶן is the Qal wayyiqtol of בָּנָה, 'and he built', with the segol that breaks up the cluster. וַיַּעַל further on is the Hiphil wayyiqtol of עָלָה, 'and he offered up': the shortening is the same in the Hiphil as in the Qal, so the stem has to be read from the vowels and the meaning.
